studies.description: Behavioral study outside the MRI scanner with 40 participants performing risky choice tasks in social contexts and reporting momentary happiness.
studies.anchor: 40 healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22 to 31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study)

studies.description: Neuroimaging study with 44 participants performing the same behavioral task during fMRI scanning.
studies.anchor: 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23 to 50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study)

protocols.description: A cooperative drawing game to create positive social bonds between participant and partner before the main task.
protocols.anchor: In this session lasting about 15 minutes, participants played an ice breaker game with their experiment partner, in which both participant and partner took turns in drawing one half of a simple picture while being blindfolded and following verbal instructions given by their game partner.

protocols.description: Main experimental task where participants chose between safe and risky monetary options across three conditions (Solo, Social, Partner).
protocols.anchor: Following the icebreaker game, participants in Study 1 performed 3 sessions of a task in which they decided on each trial between a safe and a risky monetary option (Figure 1).

protocols.description: Method to quantify risk attitudes by calculating the difference between lottery expected value and certainty equivalent.
protocols.anchor: Next, we estimated risk attitudes by calculating a risk premium for each participant and condition, defined as the difference between the expected value of a lottery and its certainty equivalent (positive values indicate risk aversion, negative values risk seeking).

protocols.description: Expected utility theory approach using constant absolute risk aversion to estimate risk attitude parameter ρ from choices.
protocols.anchor: One simple model of risk aversion termed Constant Absolute Risk Aversion (CARA) assumes an exponential utility function:

protocols.description: Five models (Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, Responsibility Redux) that explain happiness variations using rewards, prediction errors, and social comparisons.
protocols.anchor: Following previous work (Rutledge et al., 2014, 2016), we modelled the variations in momentary well-being (happiness ratings) using computational models that considered the influence of recent reward expectations, prediction errors resulting from those expectations, and differences in rewards obtained by the game partners.

protocols.description: Statistical model to test whether choices varied with expected value differences and experimental conditions.
protocols.anchor: we modelled choices with a mixed-effects logistic regression with subject-specific random intercepts u0j ∼ N(0, δu2) and slopes [u1j , u2j] ∼ N(0, δu2) and residual εij ∼ L(0, 1), assumed to follow the standard logistic distribution.

protocols.description: Neuroimaging data collection using 3T scanner and standard preprocessing including realignment, normalization, and smoothing.
protocols.anchor: Imaging data were collected on a 3T Siemens TRIO MRI system (Siemens AG, Erlangen, Germany) with a Siemens 32-channel head coil.

protocols.description: First-level GLM modeling brain responses to different trial events (choices, outcomes) across experimental conditions.
protocols.anchor: The first GLM (GLM1) included the following event types for each session: presentation of choice options, safe choice, risky choice (=lottery), receipt of outcome of safe option, all modelled separately for the Social, Partner and Solo conditions

protocols.description: Computational model-based GLM using regressors for certain rewards, expected values, and reward prediction errors from the best-fitting behavioral model.
protocols.anchor: In addition, we created another GLM (GLM2) with regressors designed to identify brain regions whose activation reflected the variables of the best-fitting computational model (see above).

protocols.description: Psychophysiological interaction analysis to identify functional connectivity changes with insula and STS seeds during decision-making.
protocols.anchor: We used the gPPI toolbox (McLaren et al., 2012) for SPM to run seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses.

protocols.description: Comparison of neural activation patterns with a published multivariate guilt-related brain signature from Yu et al. 2020.
protocols.anchor: As the GRBS and code to compare neural responses to it is freely available (https://github.com/canlab/Neuroimaging_Pattern_Masks/tree/master/Multivariate_signature_patterns/2019_Yu_Koban_Guilt), we compared this brain signature to the neural responses obtained in our task
